entities.name: Giovanni Battista Zeno
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Giovanni Battista Zeno (d. 1501-05-17) emerged as a prominent figure within the ecclesiastical hierarchy of late 15th-century Italy, primarily due to his familial connection to Pope Paul II (Pietro Barbo). Born into the powerful Venetian Zeno family, his ascent through the ranks of the Catholic Church was directly facilitated by his uncle's pontificate, positioning him as a key cardinal-nephew during a period of intense political and spiritual maneuvering in the Italian peninsula. His career spanned the cusp of the late Medieval and early Renaissance periods, reflecting the complex interplay of dynastic ambition, papal authority, and artistic patronage that characterized the Roman Curia.

Created cardinal by his uncle, Pope Paul II, on 21 November 1468, Zeno was initially appointed Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Maria in Portico Octavia, later becoming Cardinal-Priest of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere in 1470. He served as Bishop of Vicenza from 1470 until his death, though his residence was primarily in Rome, overseeing the vast financial interests and political influence associated with his cardinalate. Zeno's wealth, largely accumulated through benefices and the exploitation of his ecclesiastical offices, was substantial, allowing him to commission artworks and maintain a lavish household, typical of cardinals of his era. He participated in the conclaves of 1471 (electing Sixtus IV) and 1484 (electing Innocent VIII), and was considered a papabile candidate in both, though he never achieved the papacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Giovanni Battista Zeno's career as a cardinal-nephew and his vast accumulated wealth illustrate the pervasive nepotism and financial practices within the late 15th-century Catholic Church. His death and the subsequent appropriation of his fortune by Pope Alexander VI became a notable example of papal avarice, influencing contemporary perceptions of the Borgia papacy.
